title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

reading.body:
A lawyer submitted a legal brief containing case citations that did not exist, generated by an AI system. The citations appeared in a memorandum filed in Hennepin County Court supporting a client in a landlord-tenant dispute. The opposing attorney discovered the fabrications during a hearing, revealing that the AI had created false cases and misquoted a real one.

The failure was deploying an AI output into legal proceedings without verification. A lawyer has an ethical duty to check citations before filing them in court. Reading the cases the AI cited, or comparing them against a legal database, would have caught the nonexistent cases before they reached a judge. It is not established whether the AI system was designed or marketed as capable of generating citations, or whether the lawyer understood its limitations.

The case shows that an AI system can produce plausible-looking but entirely false legal authorities. No court can function if its filings contain fabricated precedent. The lawyer was suspended, fined, and ordered to pay costs. Whether this represents a broader pattern of lawyers using AI this way, or a rare misuse of the tool, is not established from this report alone.

reports.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

summary:
A Minnesota attorney, Faisal S. Ahmed, was suspended for 30 days after submitting false case citations generated by artificial intelligence in a 2025 legal brief filed in Hennepin County Court. Ahmed cited two nonexistent cases, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, in a memorandum supporting his client, a Robbinsdale food store owner being sued by his landlord over unpaid rent. The opposing attorney discovered the fabricated citations and false quotations from a real case during an August hearing. Judge Lois Conroy ruled against Ahmed's client, ordering $233,563 in back rent payments.

Following the discovery, Conroy fined Ahmed $5,000 and referred him to the Minnesota Lawyer's Professional Responsibility Board. Ahmed agreed to the 30-day license suspension and an additional $900 in costs. State officials emphasized that ethical obligations regarding competent legal representation apply to all use of artificial intelligence tools. This case reflects a growing problem, as over 800 documented instances of AI-generated fake legal citations have been catalogued, prompting courts nationwide to address attorney accountability when using artificial intelligence in legal filings.
